cards.title: Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture
cards.formal:
For every integer \(n\ge2\), every integer \(r\) with \(1\le r\le n-1\), and every simple loopless digraph \(D=(V,A)\) on \(n\) vertices, does
\[\bigl(\forall v\in V:\ d_D^+(v)\ge r\bigr)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\bigl(\exists\text{ a directed cycle of length }\ell\le\lceil n/r\rceil\bigr)\]
hold? Opposite arcs are allowed, and a pair of opposite arcs counts as a directed cycle of length two. The bound is exact, for every permitted pair \((n,r)\), with no additive error.
cards.definitions:
A simple loopless digraph consists of a finite set \(V\), with \(|V|=n\), and an arc set
\[A\subseteq\{(u,v)\in V\times V:u\ne v\}.\]
There is at most one copy of each ordered pair; both \((u,v)\) and \((v,u)\) may occur. Relabeling the vertices by \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) changes no requirement. The out-neighborhood and outdegree of a vertex are
\[N_D^+(v)=\{w\in V:(v,w)\in A\},\qquad d_D^+(v)=|N_D^+(v)|.\]
The minimum outdegree is \(\delta^+(D)=\min_{v\in V}d_D^+(v)\). Every vertex must meet the lower bound; an average-degree bound or a condition on only some vertices is not the hypothesis.

A directed cycle of length \(\ell\) is a sequence of pairwise distinct vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_{\ell-1}\), where \(2\le\ell\le n\), such that \((v_i,v_{i+1})\in A\) for \(0\le i<\ell-1\) and \((v_{\ell-1},v_0)\in A\). It need not be induced: additional arcs among these vertices are allowed. Length counts arcs, equivalently the number of distinct vertices on the cycle. The closing return to \(v_0\) is not counted as an additional vertex. A repeated-vertex closed walk is not the cycle witness specified here.

The directed girth \(g(D)\) is the minimum length of a directed cycle, with value \(+\infty\) if there is none. Under the positive minimum-outdegree hypothesis it is finite. The ceiling is the least integer at least the real quotient \(n/r\); equivalently, \(\lceil n/r\rceil=\lfloor(n+r-1)/r\rfloor\) for the positive integers used here. Thus the target can also be written
\[g(D)\le\lceil n/r\rceil,\quad\text{or equivalently}\quad n\ge r(g(D)-1)+1.\]
It does not assert \(g(D)\le n/r\) without rounding.

No lower bound on indegree is imposed. In particular, a graph need not be regular, strongly connected, vertex-transitive, planar or randomly generated. An oriented graph is the restricted case with no opposite pair of arcs. The target includes oriented graphs and all the other simple loopless digraphs above. This is a finite extremal existence statement, with no construction, search-algorithm, encoding or computational resource requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must cover all integers \(n,r\) in the stated ranges and all eligible digraphs, producing a cycle with the exact ceiling bound. A negative answer may specify finite \(n,r\) and a finite arc set, but must prove in Lean both the minimum-outdegree condition and the absence of every directed cycle of lengths \(2,\ldots,\lceil n/r\rceil\). A proof of the full logical negation without an explicitly listed counterexample also qualifies. An asymptotic estimate, an additive-constant relaxation, a special degree value, or an extra regularity, indegree or forbidden-subgraph hypothesis settles only a restricted statement.
cards.why: The conjecture asks whether a lower bound on every vertex’s number of outgoing neighbors forces a cycle at the sharp possible length. It would determine the exact universal relation between a local directed-degree condition and global cyclic structure. Even the dense regime that should force a directed triangle remains a major unresolved case, despite broad approximate bounds and results for symmetric graph classes.

importance.reason: A central directed-graph conjecture expressing a simple, general degree-versus-girth principle.

progress.text: Caccetta and Häggkvist formulate the exact minimum-outdegree versus directed-girth conjecture.
The primary survey records sharp examples, small-degree cases, approximate bounds and the vertex-transitive theorem.
A revised preprint claims a full proof; the present review found a failure of its stated labeling lemma and does not accept it as a resolution.
The oriented triangle threshold is improved to 0.3465 times the number of vertices.
The rainbow generalization is proved up to an additive constant depending on the fixed color-class size.
Guo’s journal article proves short rainbow-cycle results with additional color-class structure, retaining the general conjecture.
A regular-digraph preprint proves Mader’s cycle-count growth conjecture while retaining the exact degree–girth questions.
A revised rainbow-cycle paper corrects a later matroid argument and keeps its main graph result at color-class size two.

context_blocks.text: Positive minimum outdegree already guarantees that some directed cycle exists. The content of the conjecture is its exact length guarantee as the degree grows. Requiring the bound at every vertex matters: many arcs in total can coexist with acyclicity if vertices near the end of a directed ordering have small outdegree. There is no corresponding escape from the positive minimum-degree assumption.

The ceiling is essential, and the conjectured bound is sharp for every allowed \((n,r)\). The standard extremal digraph has vertices modulo \(n\), with arcs from \(i\) to \(i+1,\ldots,i+r\), using residues modulo \(n\). Its outdegree is \(r\) and its directed girth is exactly \(\lceil n/r\rceil\). These are existing extremal examples, rather than evidence that all digraphs obey the bound.

Two uses of the parameter must be distinguished. The fixed-degree case \(r=3\) is known, but the triangle-forcing regime \(r\ge n/3\) is not thereby settled. In the latter regime the degree grows with the number of vertices. For an oriented graph the conjecture predicts a directed triangle at minimum outdegree at least \(n/3\); in the more general model of this card a directed two-cycle is also an acceptable outcome.

Hladký, Král’ and Norin establish a directed triangle at minimum outdegree at least \(0.3465n\) in an oriented graph. Their paper explicitly forbids opposite arcs in its definition of “digraph.” This is a published advance toward the \(n/3\) threshold, rather than the threshold itself. The April 2026 paper still cites it as the best known partial result for this regime.

The conjecture is known for fixed minimum-degree thresholds \(r=1,2,3,4,5\), and for vertex-transitive digraphs, where an arc-preserving permutation can send any chosen vertex to any other. These successes cover substantial families but do not impose the required conclusion on an arbitrary nonsymmetric digraph. A regular graph, whose indegrees and outdegrees are all the same, need not be vertex-transitive.

Approximate girth estimates also leave a genuine exact question. Hompe and Huynh recall Shen’s universal bound \(\lceil n/r\rceil+73\). Their own 2025 article proves an additive-constant result for the stronger rainbow-cycle setting, with an error depending on the fixed color-class size. Neither additive relaxation supplies the exact ceiling required here.

A rainbow cycle has no repeated edge color. Aharoni’s conjecture asks for a short rainbow cycle in an edge-colored graph with as many color classes as vertices and sufficiently many edges in each class; the general rainbow conjecture would imply the directed conjecture. The implication is not an equivalence assertion, and a theorem for a restricted family of color classes does not establish the universal directed result.

Guo’s 2026 journal article obtains logarithmic rainbow girth when a positive fraction of the color classes have specified non-star structure, under its size conditions. An edge set is a star when all its edges meet at one vertex. Such extra structure excludes the all-star configurations relevant to the extremal directed examples. The paper explicitly retains both the directed and general rainbow conjectures as open.

Steiner’s April 2026 preprint proves a different conjecture about regular digraphs: the number of directed cycles through a common vertex, disjoint away from that vertex, must grow at least linearly with the common degree. It also proves a directed tree-width result. The introduction separately states that the exact degree–girth conjecture remains open even for regular digraphs. Counting many overlapping cycles does not itself give the sharp shortest-cycle length in this card.

The 28 July 2026 revision of the DeVos and coauthors paper retains the exact rainbow theorem for color classes of size at least two. The arXiv revision note concerns a correction in a later matroid theorem. It should not be mistaken for a newly proved all-degree Caccetta–Häggkvist theorem merely because the paper reappeared among recent revisions.

A 2008 preprint claims a complete proof, but its stated labeling lemma does not establish the required universal path bound: a small digraph passing its degree and labeling conditions violates that bound. The review records the explicit check. The later primary papers inspected here continue to state the general conjecture as open; the historical proof claim is not treated as a verified resolution.

sentences: The Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture asks how short a directed cycle must exist when every vertex has many outgoing neighbors.
For n vertices and minimum outdegree at least r, it predicts a cycle of length at most the ceiling of n divided by r.
The graph may contain opposite arcs, which form a two-cycle, but has no loops or repeated arcs.
The target is an exact theorem for every graph and degree threshold, with no extra regularity or indegree assumption.
Sharp examples and many partial results are known, while the recent rainbow and regular-digraph results do not resolve the general statement.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026 against primary sources. The inspected 2026 Guo journal article, April Steiner preprint and July DeVos et al. revision continue to retain the general conjecture. Their rainbow and regular-digraph results do not settle the exact universal target. A 2008 claimed proof was checked at its key labeling lemma, where an explicit finite counterexample to that lemma was found and recorded; it is not accepted as a resolution. No general resolution was found in the bounded later-work search, which is not exhaustive or a certification of every cited proof.

checked_sources: Read Nathanson full primary exposition, §§1–2 and Theorems 2, 7–8. Checked sharp circulant examples, small fixed-degree cases, ceiling and vertex-transitive hypothesis. Used its reported historical results with attribution, not as a fresh status check.

Read Hladký–Král’–Norin full accepted manuscript §§1–2: Theorem 1.2 threshold 0.3465 and explicit exclusion of counter-parallel arcs. Verified 2017 journal reference with the authors’ publication lists and the 2026 Steiner bibliography.

Read Hompe–Huynh v4 §1 Theorems 1.2, 1.7 and Corollary 1.8. Checked Shen’s ceiling-plus-73 statement and the fixed-r dependent rainbow additive error, and the color-class convention. Checked official May 2025 journal publication metadata.

Read He Guo full journal PDF §1 Conjectures 1–2, Theorem 4, Corollary 6 and Theorem 8. The universal directed conjecture is explicitly open; logarithmic rainbow bounds retain extra non-star structure. The source has one author, He Guo, not two authors Guo and He.

Read Steiner arXiv:2604.13700v2 §1 through the main statements: general and regular CH conjectures remain open; Theorem 3 resolves Mader’s growth question for openly disjoint cycles instead. Verified 15 April submission, 26 April revision and 28 April manuscript date separately.

Read DeVos et al. arXiv:1806.00825v4 §1 and Theorem 5; checked 28 July 2026 history and correction note. Main graph theorem is the known r=2 rainbow result; the update is not a new general resolution.

Read Mehendale arXiv:0805.3631v2 §2 labeling algorithm, Lemma 2.1 and Theorem 2.1. Independently checked the lemma on n=8,r=3 with outgoing-neighbor sets 1:{2,3,4}, 2:{3,4,5}, 3:{4,5,7}, 4:{5,7,8}, 5:{6,7,8}, 6:{1,7,8}, 7:{1,2,8}, 8:{1,2,3}. The first five labeling steps always use unlabeled targets; the newly introduced vertices are {2,3,4}, then 5, then 7, then 8, then 6. At step n-r+1=6 a backward target is necessary. All vertices have outdegree 3, with no loops or opposite arcs. Yet the shortest path from 1 to 6 has length 3, not at most ceil(8/3)-1=2 as the lemma requires: none of 1’s neighbors 2,3,4 points to 6. A BFS check confirmed these finite facts. The graph has directed triangles, so it is a counterexample only to the proof lemma, not to CH. This check is not a Lean certification or an audit of every other argument in the manuscript.

Bounded searches through 16 September 2026 checked current directed-girth, rainbow-cycle and regular-digraph results. The December 2025 Rockmael SSRN abstract treats only degree two and proposes the broader statement; no full proof reviewed. An August 2026 anti-transitive-digraph article is explicitly a special-class result. No accepted general resolution found; search is not exhaustive.
quality_review.scope: Checked target, definitions, quantifiers, answer criterion, context, significance and dated source claims. Bounded later-work checks do not independently certify every cited proof.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
